say.text: Welcome to class two: life in a medieval village. Some of what we say is REAL history. Some is INVENTED for Nimrod. We will label every part.

show.text: Life in a Medieval Village: REAL history and INVENTED Nimrod

say.text: First, who lived in the real medieval countryside? Picture ten people. Around nine of them worked the land. Estimates run from about 80 to 90 out of every 100.

show.text: REAL: about 9 in every 10 people lived by farming

ask.q: Out of ten people in medieval Europe, about how many worked the land?
ask.right: About eight or nine
wrong: None of them; most were knights
ask.why: Historians estimate that around 80 to 90 percent of people were farmers or peasants. Knights and lords were a small group.

say.text: Those farmers lived on a manor. A manor was an estate controlled by a lord. The village sat nearby, with houses, barns and animal pens close together.

show.text: MANOR: an estate run by a lord, worked by the people of the village

ask.q: What was a manor?
ask.right: An estate controlled by a lord, worked by the villagers
wrong: A tall tower at the corner of a castle
A market for buying magic goods
ask.why: The manor was the centre of work and life. The lord controlled it and the peasants farmed it.

say.text: Now the land itself. Around most villages lay three big fields. Two grew crops each year. The third was left fallow, which means resting with nothing planted.

show.text: REAL: the three fields in one year

ask.q: A village has three fields. How many are planted in one year?
ask.right: Two
ask.why: Two fields grow crops and one rests. Next year the jobs rotate.

say.text: Why was the three-field way a big deal? Older villages often used two fields and rested half the land. Let us count it for a village of 60 acres.

show.text: REAL: acres planted each year, 60-acre village

ask.q: A village has 60 acres split into three equal fields. With two fields planted, how many acres are planted?
ask.right: 40 acres
ask.why: Each field is 20 acres. Two planted fields make 40 acres. That is a third more than the 30 acres planted with two fields.

say.text: The fields were cut into long strips. Good land and poor land were mixed, so each family held strips in all three fields.

show.text: A big open field divided into long narrow strips, with each family's strips scattered among their neighbours' strips

ask.q: Why did each family get strips in all three fields?
ask.right: So everyone had a fair share of the good land
wrong: So they could sell the strips to the king
So no field ever needed to rest
So the lord could count them more easily
ask.why: Spreading each family's strips across all the fields shared out the good and poor land.

say.text: So the farming year was a loop. Fields were ploughed three times. There were sowings in autumn and in spring. Animals grazed the common land. At harvest, workers were fed bread and some cheese.

show.text: REAL farming year: plough three times | sow in autumn and spring | graze animals on common land | harvest | store the grain

say.text: What did people eat? Mostly dark bread, a thick stew called pottage, and weak ale. Meat was a treat, often bacon from the family pig.

show.text: REAL food: dark bread | pottage (a thick stew of grain, peas and vegetables) | weak ale | cheese and dairy | meat as a treat

ask.q: What was pottage?
ask.right: A thick stew of grain, peas or vegetables
ask.why: Pottage was the pot that was always on the fire. It went with bread and ale at most meals.

say.text: Now homes. Walls were a timber frame filled with wattle and daub. Wattle is woven sticks, often hazel or willow. Daub is a sticky plaster that covers them. The roof was thatch.

show.text: A low timber-framed cottage with walls of woven sticks covered in clay plaster and a thick straw roof

ask.q: What is wattle and daub?
ask.right: Woven sticks covered with a sticky plaster, used to fill the walls
ask.why: Wattle is the woven stick lattice. Daub is the plaster covering it.

say.text: One Welsh farmhouse from about 1470 to 1500 had an earth floor and a fire in the hall. The smoke left through windows with no glass. A cowhouse sat at the other end of the building. Very few small houses like it survive.

show.text: Inside a long farmhouse: a hall with a central fire, beaten earth floor, no glass in the windows, and a cowhouse at one end

say.text: Not everyone only farmed. A village also had a blacksmith, a miller, bakers, and alewives. Alewives brewed and sold ale, and in many English villages they were mostly women.

show.text: REAL village jobs: farmer | blacksmith (nails, horseshoes, tools) | miller (grain into flour) | baker | alewife (brews and sells ale)

ask.q: Who brewed and sold ale in many English villages?
ask.right: Alewives, usually women
ask.why: Ale spoiled quickly, so villagers made and sold it in small batches. Local records suggest that nearly every adult woman in a village took part.

say.text: Now power. A lord owned or controlled the manor. Many peasants were serfs: tied to the land and not free to leave without the lord's permission. A serf was not a slave, because serfs were not bought and sold.

show.text: LORD and SERF: the lord controls the manor; the serf works the land and needs permission to leave

ask.q: Could a serf move away whenever they chose?
ask.right: No, they needed the lord's permission
ask.why: Serfs lacked freedom of movement. They also needed permission for things like marriage.

say.text: It worked like a trade. Peasants gave labour, rent and a share of what they grew. The lord gave protection, justice and land to farm.

show.text: REAL. Peasants gave: work on the lord's land, rent, a share of produce || The lord gave: protection, justice, land to farm

ask.q: Which of these did the lord give in return for the peasants' work?
ask.right: Protection
wrong: The whole harvest of the king's fields
ask.why: The lord gave protection, a way to get justice, and the right to farm certain fields.

say.text: Lords had bosses too. A vassal received land and owed their lord military service, advice and money. So power ran up a ladder to the king. In Nimrod, that king is King Kenny.

show.text: The ladder. REAL: king | great lords | lesser lords and knights (vassals) | peasants. INVENTED: King Kenny sits at the top of Nimrod's ladder

ask.q: What did a vassal owe the lord who gave them land?
ask.right: Military service, advice and financial support
wrong: Only a promise to be friendly
ask.why: Vassals held land from a lord. In return they owed fighting, counsel and money.

say.text: Now, where is our picture too simple? Many people think the Middle Ages were a 'dark' time with no progress. Many historians dislike that label. Later thinkers made it up to make their own age look brighter.

show.text: TOO SIMPLE #1: 'The Dark Ages'

ask.q: Why do many historians avoid the label 'Dark Ages'?
ask.right: It is misleading, and later thinkers invented it to make their own time look better
wrong: Because medieval people had no farms
Because it was invented by medieval peasants
Because every record from that time was lost
ask.why: The label is seen as an oversimplified idea. Some writers made the Middle Ages look dark to make their own era look advanced.

say.text: The word 'feudalism' is debated too. Medieval people never used it. In 1974 historian Elizabeth Brown argued it was a construct made by later scholars. Some historians now use 'feudalism' for lords and vassals, and 'manorialism' for lords and peasants.

show.text: TOO SIMPLE #2: 'feudalism' (still debated)

ask.q: Why do many historians use the word 'feudalism' with care?
ask.right: Medieval people did not use it, and one label can hide how different places really were
wrong: It is a spell word from old stories
It means only castles and knights
ask.why: Many historians think the single label is too simple for the real web of relationships in medieval Europe.

say.text: And peasants were not all the same. Some were free farmers. Serfs' duties varied a lot, from a few days a year to about three days a week. Towns could offer a way out: a serf who stayed a year and a day uncaught could become free.

show.text: TOO SIMPLE #3: all peasants were the same | free farmers existed | serf duties varied by place and time | in towns, a serf might become free after a year and a day

ask.q: True or false: every peasant had exactly the same duties everywhere in medieval Europe.
ask.right: False. Duties and freedom varied by place and time
wrong: True. The rules were identical in every village
False, but only because the king changed them daily
ask.why: There were free farmers as well as serfs. Duties could be light or heavy depending on time and place.

say.text: Now we step into Nimrod village. From here, what we say is INVENTED. We borrow real details from what we just learned so it feels true.

show.text: INVENTED: a day in Nimrod village

say.text: INVENTED: Jack is a village farmer. He works strips in all three fields. At dawn he eats bread, ploughs his strips, and some days works the lord's land. At night it is pottage by the fire.

show.text: INVENTED day for Jack: dawn: bread and ale | morning: plough his strips | some days: work on the lord's land | afternoon: animals on the common land | evening: pottage by the fire

ask.q: Which real fact explains why Jack has strips in all three fields?
ask.right: Families got strips in every field for a fair share of good land
wrong: Every serf was ordered to plant dragons' eggs
Jack is rich enough to buy the whole village
ask.why: In real villages, strips were shared out across all three fields. Jack's day copies that.

say.text: INVENTED: Dame Gladys is the village alewife. Ale spoils in a few days, so she brews small batches often. She sells to neighbours and hears all the news.

show.text: INVENTED day for Dame Gladys: brew a small batch | sell to neighbours | trade news | save barley for the next brew. REAL link: alewives, and ale that spoiled within days

ask.q: Why would Gladys brew fresh ale again and again?
ask.right: Ale spoiled quickly and had to be drunk within a few days
wrong: The king ordered a new batch every night
ask.why: Ale did not keep. That is why many villages had alewives making and selling small batches.

say.text: INVENTED: Robin the Joker has no strips of his own. He performs at feasts and at the castle. His jokes can say what others dare not. Real court fools did something like this.

show.text: INVENTED day for Robin: tell jokes at the alehouse | perform at feasts | carry news | speak truth through humour. REAL link: court fools were entertainers and sometimes clever advisers

ask.q: Besides making people laugh, what could real court jesters sometimes do?
ask.right: Advise rulers and criticise them under the cover of humour
wrong: Collect the rent for the lord
ask.why: Many jesters were intelligent and trusted advisers. Humour let them comment on the nobles' behaviour.

say.text: Now a thought experiment, like in class one. The question is: what happens to Nimrod village if one harvest fails? We change one thing and keep everything else the same.

show.text: Thought experiment: what if one harvest fails?

say.text: First, a real clue. Between 1000 and 1347, Europe's population grew from about 35 to 80 million. With so many people, there was little spare food, so even a small shortfall could hurt.

show.text: 35 million to 80 million (Europe, 1000 to 1347)

ask.q: Why could a slightly poor harvest around 1315 cause hunger?
ask.right: There were so many people that there was little spare food
wrong: Fields were too small to plough
Nobody knew how to bake bread
All the farmers had left for the cities
ask.why: The population was at a high, so any shortfall in the harvest could have severe results.

say.text: Second, count the grain. One source says that in the 1200s a farmer might get up to ten bushels for each one sown. In the Great Famine that fell by a third to a half. We keep one bushel to plant again.

show.text: Grain back per 1 sown: a good year and the famine years

ask.q: A good year gives 10 back for each 1 sown. The harvest is cut by half. How many do you get back?
ask.why: Half of 10 is 5. Keep 1 to plant next year and only 4 are left to eat and to pay dues.

say.text: Now the chain reaction in Nimrod. All of this is INVENTED, based on real patterns. Jack must choose between eating his grain and saving seed. Gladys has less grain for ale. Robin's neighbours have little to spare. King Kenny gets less, and hungry people grow angry.

show.text: INVENTED chain: Jack: eat now or keep seed? | Gladys: weaker ale | Robin: fewer feasts, fewer coins | King Kenny: less rent, angry villagers. REAL link: weaker ale and thinner pottage when grain ran short; famine brought class conflict and unrest

ask.q: Jack harvests far less grain than he hoped. What hard choice does he face?
ask.right: Eat the grain now, or save some as seed for next year's crop
wrong: Whether to turn the grain into gold
Whether to move the three fields into two
ask.why: If he eats all the grain, he has nothing to plant. If he saves seed, he goes hungrier now.

say.text: What really happened? In 1315, heavy rain ruined harvests across northern Europe. It was not one bad year: bad weather lasted into 1317, and animals fell sick. About 5 to 12 out of every 100 people in northern Europe died. Recovery took years.

show.text: REAL: about 5 to 12 in every 100 died in the Great Famine of 1315 to 1317

ask.q: What made the Great Famine so deadly, beyond one failed harvest?
ask.right: Harvests failed over several years, animals sickened, and food was already tight
wrong: One failed harvest always killed half of Europe
The farmers forgot to leave a field fallow
ask.why: Wet weather lasted from 1315 into 1317, and disease hit animals. The population was large, so there was little spare food.

say.text: Let us finish by sorting REAL from INVENTED. Real: three fields, serfs, lords, famine. Invented: Jack, Gladys, Robin and King Kenny. Next class, we go inside the castle.

show.text: REAL: three fields, one fallow | bread, pottage, ale | lords and serfs, with duties both ways | the Great Famine. INVENTED: Jack, Dame Gladys, Robin, King Kenny. TOO SIMPLE: 'Dark Ages' and 'feudalism'

ask.q: Which of these is INVENTED?
ask.right: Dame Gladys brewing ale for Nimrod village
wrong: Villages had three fields, with one fallow each year
Serfs needed permission to leave the manor
The Great Famine began with heavy rain in 1315
ask.why: Nimrod village and its people are invented. The other three are real history.

notes.topic: Editor note: the course notes do not say what Jack, Robin the Joker or Dame Gladys do. This lesson assumes Jack is a village farmer, Gladys is the village alewife and Robin is a joker who performs at feasts and at the castle. Mike to confirm or change these.

Editor note on sources: no OpenStax chapter was read for this lesson. Several sources are general education or history websites, not academic works, and some give no date. The Welsh farmhouse record (s10) is from a national heritage body. The Great Famine book page (s8) is from a university press, but only its description was read. Figures such as peasant share of population and grain yields are estimates and differ between sources.

frame_of_reference.when: 1315 to 1317: the Great Famine in northern Europe
frame_of_reference.elsewhere: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, set out on a pilgrimage to Mecca. In 1325 the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta set out on his own journey east. In the same year the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan.

frame_of_reference.when: The mid-1300s: the Black Death followed the famine
frame_of_reference.elsewhere: The plague also struck North Africa and Central Asia, not only Europe.

other_side.claim: Medieval society was a clear 'feudal system' with the king at the top and the peasants at the bottom.
other_side.other_view: Elizabeth Brown argued in 1974 that 'feudalism' is a later construct that oversimplifies medieval life. Many medieval historians dislike the word. Others still use it, often limiting it to the lord-vassal bond and calling the lord-peasant bond manorialism.

Britannica stresses that serfs lacked freedoms such as moving, marrying or changing job without the lord's permission. A popular history site argues that serfdom gave more freedom and stability than we assume, with duties that could be light. Obligations varied by time and place, so both views can be partly right. The second source is less academic.

other_side.claim: The Middle Ages were a 'dark age' with little progress.
other_side.other_view: Scholars debate the idea, and many reject the label. Some defend it only for the earliest part of the period.

other_side.claim: In a good medieval year, a farmer got about ten grains back for each one sown.
other_side.other_view: One source uses a figure of up to ten. Another gives about seven in a good year and about two in a bad one. The exact numbers vary by source, so the lesson's chart is a teaching model, not an exact measure.
